title: Running a Thousand Miles for Freedom; or, The Escape of William and Ellen Craft from Slavery (1860)
inspectedText: The retrospective first-person narrative says Ellen would impersonate an ill white gentleman and William his enslaved attendant. It explicitly identifies inability to write as a problem. Ellen proposes binding her right hand so others could register her name; facial bandages conceal her beardless chin. The account explains the male role in relation to travel conventions, not merely complexion. Conversation avoidance and a familiar passenger create risk. In Charleston an official refuses to sign for her; apparent acquaintanceship and the steamer captain's intervention help. Baltimore officials demand security before allowing an enslaved passenger north; the account attributes eventual passage to the conductor confirming their prior journey, departure pressure and sympathy for the apparently ill gentleman. They reach Philadelphia, remove the disguise and obtain abolitionist support. Exact dialogue is retrospective testimony, not a recorded transcript. The date/weekday combination in line437 needs reconciliation; omit fine dates at this gate. The surrounding unrelated anecdotes and broad legal assertions have not been verified or adopted.
sourceQualityRationale: Primary participant account published about twelve years after escape, with abolitionist rhetorical purpose. Digital transcription, not an inspected first-edition facsimile. Strong direct evidence for their explanation of the disguise, insufficient alone for verbatim dialogue or all legal/history details.
